The Bill, the Bombs, and the Border: A Week That Rewrote the Ledger

Congress passed the largest fiscal package of Trump's second term while the Supreme Court narrowed judicial oversight and immigration enforcement expanded on multiple fronts

```markdown The week beginning June 28 and closing on Independence Day was defined by two intertwined stories: a sweeping fiscal and immigration bill that moved from contested procedure to presidential signature in seven days, and a steady narrowing of the judiciary's capacity to check executive action. Around those twin currents ran a dense set of enforcement actions, press pressure, and public dissent that gave the week its full shape.

The weekend opened with the Supreme Court's ruling that lower courts generally cannot issue nationwide injunctions, a decision arising from a challenge to Trump's executive order narrowing birthright citizenship. The 6-3 ruling did not settle whether the underlying order was constitutional, but it allowed enforcement to proceed unevenly, state by state, while litigation continued elsewhere—stripping courts of a tool they had used to halt contested policies nationwide in a single stroke.

That same weekend, the administration ended Temporary Protected Status for roughly half a million Haitians, and a Justice Department directive prioritizing denaturalization of naturalized citizens accused of crimes began drawing scrutiny. Both moves expanded executive discretion over who could claim secure legal standing in the country. Separately, following the earlier U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, the Senate voted 53-47 along party lines to reject a resolution that would have required congressional authorization for further military action, leaving decisions about escalation concentrated in the presidency. In the Senate, meanwhile, the reconciliation bill cleared its first procedural votes 51-49, even as the parliamentarian ruled several provisions—including Medicaid-related additions—out of order, previewing a fight over substance that would run through the entire week. ICE actions over the weekend detained the father, wife, and daughter of military veterans, and a deceased veteran's son, while Trump endorsed legislation to strip tax-exempt status from nonprofits linked to protests. Nationwide "No Kings" demonstrations drew millions of participants, and in Louisiana a Catholic school fired a longtime teacher after learning of his marriage to a man.

By Monday, the fight over the budget bill escalated sharply. Trump urged Senate Republicans to disregard the parliamentarian's rulings outright, and the chamber passed the bill 51-50, with Vice President Vance breaking the tie. Senators also voted to treat $3.8 trillion in tax cuts as costing nothing for scoring purposes—a maneuver that altered the accounting rules meant to constrain how sweeping fiscal legislation can pass. The same day brought a wave of arrests involving sitting officials: Senator Alex Padilla, Newark Mayor Ras Baraka, New York City Comptroller Brad Lander, and Representative LaMonica McIver were all detained in episodes connected to ICE facility visits and protests, following the earlier arrest of Wisconsin Judge Hannah Dugan. Taken together, these arrests raised serious concerns about law enforcement being used against officials engaged in oversight of executive conduct.

Courts pushed back on multiple fronts that same Monday. Sixteen Democratic attorneys general sued over cancelled school mental health funds, a federal judge blocked mass firings at HHS, and another judge blocked the termination of Haitian TPS. Reports also surfaced of overcrowded, inhumane conditions inside ICE facilities, and a 75-year-old Cuban detainee died in custody—the thirteenth such death of the fiscal year. Elsewhere, Trump lifted select Syria sanctions by executive order, while Delaware enacted the Freedom to Read Act limiting book bans. A different kind of pressure also began to surface: more than 600 EPA employees signed a formal dissent against agency policy, DHS's border czar urged investigating CNN over its coverage of an ICE-tracking app, and the administration warned Harvard over antisemitism compliance—an early signal of the funding and investigative leverage that would recur throughout the week.

Tuesday carried the bill to Senate passage. Republicans approved the reconciliation package with Vice President Vance again breaking a tie, sending it to the House. The bill extended the 2017 tax cuts, funded mass deportations, and cut Medicaid and SNAP, with the Congressional Budget Office projecting a $3.3 trillion increase in the deficit through 2034. The same day, Florida opened the Alligator Alcatraz detention facility in the Everglades, built with capacity for up to 1,000 detainees and expandable to 5,000, prompting an immediate environmental lawsuit over the absence of required review. Press pressure intensified in parallel: Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said the Justice Department was considering prosecuting CNN over its ICEBlock app coverage, while Trump separately threatened action over Iran-related reporting. In an unrelated but consequential development, Paramount agreed to pay Trump $16 million to settle a lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview—two distinct pressure points on the press arising the same day through different channels. The administration also froze $6.8 billion in congressionally appropriated K-12 funding covering after-school, English-learner, and adult education programs, testing the limits of executive discretion over money Congress had already approved. A federal appeals court rejected the detention of Georgetown scholar Badar Khan Suri during deportation proceedings, and Trump threatened to cut government subsidies to Elon Musk's companies amid their public feud. The University of Pennsylvania, meanwhile, announced new restrictions on transgender athletes in women's sports and erased Lia Thomas's swimming records, following an agreement with the administration.

Wednesday centered on a chaotic House effort to adopt the Senate's bill without amendment. Trump pressured wavering Republicans directly, including with threats of primary challengers, while House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries delivered a record eight-hour floor speech opposing the legislation. The bill was ultimately adopted after a marathon procedural vote kept open for hours. The same day, a federal judge ruled that Trump's proclamation of an "invasion" at the border, and the resulting asylum ban, exceeded presidential authority, giving the administration fourteen days to seek emergency relief—a reaffirmation of statutory limits on unilateral executive control over asylum access. A coalition of twenty states led by California's attorney general sued over the sharing of Medicaid enrollee data with DHS for immigration enforcement purposes, alleging privacy violations. Trump called for investigating former DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas and threatened to arrest New York mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani over unfounded citizenship claims, while separately suggesting that U.S. citizens who commit crimes should be deported—rhetoric that blurred constitutional boundaries around citizenship itself. In a smaller but telling episode, officers attempted to deport Ward Sakeik, a stateless Palestinian woman, despite a standing court order barring her removal; her belongings were placed outside her cell before the attempt was halted. Gail Lee, known for challenging voter registrations, was appointed to DeKalb County's elections board, and Trump visited the newly opened Florida detention facility.

Thursday brought the bill's final congressional passage. Following Jeffries' speech, the House gave final approval, sending the legislation to Trump's desk with its $3.3 trillion projected deficit increase, cuts to Medicaid, SNAP, and green energy incentives, and expanded immigration enforcement funding intact. The Supreme Court's conservative majority separately allowed the deportation of eight men to South Sudan to proceed, despite concerns about torture risk, overruling a lower court that had required a chance to contest such removals—a ruling that extended the same term's earlier curtailment of nationwide injunctions into a direct narrowing of protection for individuals facing removal to third countries. The Court also agreed to hear cases on state bans on transgender athletes and reaffirmed a ruling allowing parents to opt children out of LGBTQ+-themed school lessons, adding new fronts to an already active docket. On the ground, a 64-year-old Iranian woman with no criminal record was detained in New Orleans after decades of residency, and a citizen photographer filed a $1 million claim after being arrested while filming an ICE raid—two enforcement episodes distinct in character but united in showing how far the crackdown's reach extended.

Independence Day brought the week's culmination. At a White House ceremony, Trump signed the reconciliation bill into law as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, permanently extending the 2017 tax cuts, funding a $170 billion expansion of immigration enforcement, cutting Medicaid and SNAP, phasing out clean energy incentives, and raising the debt ceiling by $5 trillion. It was the completion of an arc that had run continuously from Saturday's procedural votes through a parliamentarian override, a tie-breaking vice-presidential vote, and a pressured House majority. The same day, five Democratic lawmakers were blocked from inspecting the Alligator Alcatraz facility, closing the loop on a site that had opened under environmental objection and now resisted legislative oversight. A Los Angeles school district demanded a federal investigation after ICE agents were filmed urinating on high school grounds before a raid. Ward Sakeik, the stateless Palestinian woman twice targeted for removal despite a court order, was released from custody after four months, following sustained legal effort by her and her American husband. And across the country, the 50501 Movement organized mutual-aid and community events for the holiday, a grassroots counterpoint to a week otherwise dominated by concentrated federal action.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a government moving with unusual speed and coordination across its legislative, executive, and judicial branches toward a single outcome: a larger, more heavily funded enforcement apparatus paired with a smaller social safety net, achieved partly by setting aside the procedural friction normally built into each institution. The Senate's disregard for its own parliamentarian, the House's adoption of the bill under direct presidential pressure, and the Supreme Court's narrowing of the injunctions and protections traditionally available to litigants each removed a distinct brake on the exercise of power. Yet the week did not pass unopposed. Federal judges blocked firings and TPS terminations even as Congress advanced its bill; state attorneys general filed suit over data-sharing practices; agency employees signed public dissents; sitting officials were arrested for acts of oversight, and their arrests themselves became public controversies; and ordinary citizens organized protests and community events on the very day the legislation was signed. The result was a week in which the concentration of federal power and the persistence of institutional and civic resistance advanced side by side, leaving the country's checks strained but not silent. ```
